summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, restricting trans people's use of public bathrooms; the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private and public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination in Peru, according to Outright International's current country overview, so official channels are not reliably protective for a trans visitor who reports an incident.

An April 2025 law on foreign funding for NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order' and 'security' grounds, which Outright International assesses risks being weaponised against queer organising. Combined with the censorship articles in the sexual-integrity law, the space for advocacy that a visitor might rely on for support is narrowing.

The bathroom restriction is comparable to measures passed in other countries, and the removal of LGBT hate-crime coverage in 2017 places Peru alongside only Paraguay and Guyana in South America in lacking such statutory protection.

Pride marches have been held annually in Peru since 2002, with a recorded march as early as 1984, indicating visible community presence alongside the documented risk.

Community demands recorded alongside the bathroom bills include reliable HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.
localsOnly:
Health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance in June 2024, a change directed at residents navigating healthcare settings rather than at visitors.

A 2012 study by the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a structural fact shaping economic and policing exposure for trans residents.

The bathroom legislation also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity' in public facilities, affecting everyday use of schools, workplaces and public buildings for trans residents.

Congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at the Instituto Nacional Materno Perinatal, an issue raised by trans and feminist organisers alongside the LGBTIQ+ demands.

The 2017 repeal of LGBT hate-crime coverage means residents must rely on general criminal provisions rather than an aggravating ground for bias-motivated violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The bill numbers are reported inconsistently across sources: one account cites bills 6506 and 8457 approved in committee in February 2025, another cites 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR approved by Congress in April 2025. Which instrument carried the bathroom restriction through to law is unresolved in the material reviewed.

Whether the February 2025 committee dictamen was enacted independently of the April 2025 sexual-integrity law, and whether the bathroom provision has been challenged in court, is not sourced here.

Enforcement practice of the biological-sex restroom rule, including whether security staff or public authorities have applied it against visitors, is not documented in the material reviewed.

The figure of 54 transgender and gender-diverse people killed between 2020 and 2023, and the report of a consumer-protection body dismissing a trans woman's complaint against a gym, are carried from the record without a source attached in this inventory; both remain unverified here.

Whether the 17-year sentence against the three officers has been appealed, and whether the officers remained in custody pending appeal, is not stated in the sources reviewed.
